newsitem.title: GREECE: Greece says no to EU-proposed meeting with Turkey.
newsitem.headline: Greece says no to EU-proposed meeting with Turkey.

text.p: Greece rejected on Friday a European Union proposal calling on Greek and Turkish experts to meet this month to help resolve thorny differences between the two Balkan neighbours.

Foreign Minister Theodoros Pangalos told reporters Greece would not send its experts to a meeting on May 26-28 in the Netherlands, proposed by Dutch Foreign Minister Hans Van Mierlo, current head of the EU general affairs council.
"It takes two to tango," Pangalos said. "Mr Van Mierlo must understand that he made a mistake and what he said (the meeting) can't take place ... it will be pointless."

NATO allies Greece and Turkey agreed last month to each set up a committee of experts to discuss procedures on ways to tackle long-standing problems, including territorial feuds in the Aegean Sea separating the two countries.
But Greece's Socialist Prime Minister Costas Simitis came under intense pressure from senior members of his party who said they would not endorse any negotiations with Ankara.
The government then said the two committees would not meet face-to-face but exchange letters with their views through the EU.
"We are about ready to sent the text (with the Greek positions) on condition that this request for a meeting be withdrawn as it creates problems to the whole procedure," Pangalos said.

Pangalos reiterated that any rapprochement with Turkey at this point did not mean that Athens would lift its veto within the EU blocking millions of dollars in aid to Ankara as part of a customs union between Turkey and the EU.

He has said Turkey must first renounce threats of war against Greece, talks should begin on the accession of the divided island of Cyprus to the EU and territorial differences in the Aegean should be resolved through international courts.
Despite the setback over the experts' meeting, it is the first time since January last year that the two neighbours have considered talking to each other even through letters to a third body.
They had then come close to war over ownership of two uninhabited islets in the eastern Aegean.
Greece and Turkey have long been at odds over rights in the Aegean, Cyprus and a Moslem minority in northern Greece.
